new_statements.quote: It is difficult to pronounce on the tones of a language without an intimate knowledge of it, which I do not possess in the case of Taman ... As far as I can ascertain there are only two tones, the high (¯) and the low (_). One of these appears in the word for "water," which is t'i_, while that for egg is t'i¯. Some other words with the same ending may be pronounced with indifference in either tone. Thus vi, a dog, may be pronounced either vi¯ or vi_ without altering the meaning. ... The Burmese check tone appears to be absent. The final vowel is often short, even when accented, but this is the case in French, and is quite a different thing from the sharp closure of the glottis, combined with a falling tone, which is found in Burmese.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Brown describes Taman as a tone language with two tones (high, low; a falling-tone diacritic also appears in his key) and a low functional load (some words vary freely between tones); he makes no statement about the position of word stress — the only mention of accent is the passing remark that a final vowel is often short 'even when accented'.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; for tone, Brown notes some words (e.g. vi 'dog') may take either tone without change of meaning. Huziwara 2016 (sec. 2.4, p.9) adds that Brown's list actually contains no high-tone examples, one low-tone word and ten falling-tone words with no minimal pairs, so the reliability of the tone marking is unknown.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms in a 75-item wordlist (mostly monosyllables and sesquisyllables) elicited by a colonial administrator ca. 1910; no connected speech. The language is extinct (last speakers 1990s per Huziwara 2016); Huziwara's 2015 rememberer data are transcribed 'ignoring tone' and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Brown's data are from Tamans of the Htamanthi (Tamanthi) area, Upper Chindwin, ca. 1910 — the variety Glottolog codes as tama1328 / ISO tcl. Not to be confused with Taman of Borneo (tama1335, Austronesian). Brown mentions a closely similar undocumented neighbour 'Malin'.

sources.citation: Huziwara, Keisuke [藤原敬介]. 2016. タマン語の系統再考 (On the genetic position of Taman reconsidered). Kyoto University Linguistic Research 35: 1-34. doi:10.14989/219018
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 2 (音韻論) re-analyses Brown's 75-word list: syllable structure C1GVC2, consonants, vowels; sec. 2.4 声調 (p.9): tone probably distinctive but Brown's marking gives no high-tone examples, one low-tone word, 10 falling-tone words, no minimal pairs, reliability unknown; n.26: Luce 1985 drops the accent (tone) marks. Sec. 4: a few words and a song from an 83-year-old rememberer (2015) in simplified transcription 'ignoring tone'. Nothing on stress. States Brown 1911 is the only Taman material and the last speakers died in the 1990s.
